Mask-Placement Robustness in AI-Assisted Painting Restoration

Multi-model sensitivity to location, geometry, and component arrangement under matched damaged area
Controlled 50-painting dataset · five-painting mask-robustness subset · standalone self-contained report

1. What was evaluated?

This report measures input-mask robustness: how strongly restoration evidence changes when a valid damage mask moves or changes shape while its damaged area remains approximately matched. The experiment contains five paintings, three fixed family–area conditions, five variants per group, 75 cases, and 225 preselected restorations.

5paintings
15matched robustness groups
75mask-variant cases
225restoration candidates
11quality anchors
3restoration methods

The design is large enough to expose whether a result depends on one convenient mask placement. The five paintings—not the 75 cases—remain the independent units, so conclusions apply to this controlled evidence population rather than paintings in general.

2. Were mask variants genuinely different?

Yes. Every painting–condition group contains five masks with distinct pixels, positions, and morphology signatures. The largest absolute difference between requested and realized damaged area was 0.0123 percentage points.

The masks changed where and how damage appeared without materially changing the requested area. Differences observed later therefore represent sensitivity to mask realization within each fixed family–area condition, rather than simple area mismatch.

3. How much did measured quality change between variants?

Within-group median absolute deviation was computed separately for all eleven quality anchors. Lower dispersion means that the measured result changed less when a different valid mask was used.

model_id Quality anchor Telea MAD LaMa MAD Stable Diffusion MAD Lowest descriptive MAD
Masked MAE 1.3449 0.8048 2.4454 LaMa
Masked ΔE 0.3372 0.6177 0.8031 OpenCV Telea
CLIP crop 0.0043 0.0014 0.0054 LaMa
DINOv2 crop 0.0092 0.0038 0.0303 LaMa
LPIPS crop 0.0125 0.0073 0.0159 LaMa
Boundary seam 0.0007 0.0006 0.0018 LaMa

Structural affinity 0.0098 0.0017 0.0128 LaMa
SSIM crop 0.0083 0.0087 0.0168 OpenCV Telea
Texture error p95 0.0122 0.0280 0.4234 OpenCV Telea

LaMa had the lowest descriptive MAD on 8 of 11 anchors, Telea on 3, and Stable Diffusion on 0. This makes LaMa the broadest descriptive robustness leader in this experiment. However, none of the 132 paired comparisons survived FDR correction, so the available five-painting evidence does not establish a statistically clear model difference.

Low dispersion is not the same as good restoration quality. A method can reproduce a consistently poor result across masks and still look robust by this measure.

4. What did restorations look like across variants?

The following panels retain the approved damaged-input-plus-three-model layout for all five variants. They provide visual context for the numeric robustness results.

  • In the displayed thin-scratch group, LaMa usually removes the narrow line with the cleanest local continuation.
  • Telea often repairs the scratch but can introduce local smoothing.
  • Stable Diffusion retains visible grey linear traces in several displayed scratch variants, matching the limitation identified during its restoration-stage review.
  • Larger missing regions allow plausible but invented content, especially for the diffusion model.

The visual evidence supports the metric result that model behaviour can change with mask placement. It does not establish historical authenticity or conservation suitability.

5. Which model was most stable overall?

Two complementary summaries were retained: anchor-specific dispersion and family-balanced variant ranking. They are shown separately rather than merged into a combined quality or trust score.

Model Top-ranked variants Fraction of 75 variants
OpenCV Telea 20 0.2667
LaMa 55 0.7333
Stable Diffusion 0 0.0000

LaMa was top-ranked for 55 of 75 variants, Telea for 20, and Stable Diffusion for 0. Descriptively, LaMa was the most consistently preferred method, Telea was second, and Stable Diffusion was never the overall leader in this controlled population.

This is comparative computational evidence, not a conservation approval. Family-balanced ranking prevents a large metric family from dominating, but it remains dependent on the approved metric set.

6. Did the preferred model change with mask realization?

Yes. Several painting–condition groups changed their top-ranked model or anchor-specific winner when another valid mask realization was used.

The most stable group changed the preferred model for 0 of 11 anchors, while the most sensitive group changed it for 9 of 11. A comparison based on only one mask can therefore be dependable for some images and fragile for others.

7. Which evidence families were most mask-sensitive?

Winner agreement was measured independently for pixel, perceptual, feature, spatial, texture, colour, seam, semantic, and structural anchors.

No single evidence family was uniformly stable across every painting and mask condition. Feature, semantic, structural, colour, seam, and pixel evidence can disagree about which restoration is preferable. A trustworthy evaluation must therefore retain metric disagreement instead of presenting one metric as the answer.

9. Did robustness differ by mask family?

Descriptive profiles differed between thin scratches, small losses, and large losses.

Mask condition Median anchors changing winner Median changed fraction Observed range
Thin scratch · fixed at 2% 8.0000 0.7273 0.18–0.82
Small loss · fixed at 4.5% 3.0000 0.2727 0.00–0.27
Large loss · fixed at 12.5% 5.0000 0.4545 0.27–0.82

The highest median winner-change fraction occurred for Thin scratch · fixed at 2%. This condition was the least stable descriptively, but it cannot be attributed to mask family alone because every family is paired with one fixed damaged area.

Thin scratches are fixed at 2%, small losses at 4.5%, and large losses at 12.5%. Family and damage size are therefore confounded by design. Notebook 23 remains the canonical damage-size analysis.

10. Painting-specific robustness

Robustness was not identical across the five paintings. The analysis therefore preserves painting-level profiles rather than treating all 75 cases as independent artworks.

Painting Median changed fraction Minimum Maximum

p018 0.2727 0.2727 0.8182

p001 had the highest median fraction of anchors changing winner, while p026 had the lowest. Mask sensitivity therefore depends partly on the specific image content, and one representative painting is not enough for a model-level conclusion.

11. Runtime and operational stability

Runtime variation was measured across the same five mask variants but was excluded from all quality rankings.

Model Median runtime MAD (s) CI lower CI upper
LaMa 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000
OpenCV Telea 0.0060 0.0039 0.0124
Stable Diffusion 0.0139 0.0116 0.0752

Stable Diffusion showed the largest recorded runtime variation, while Telea varied less. LaMa has zero recorded within-group MAD because its persisted runtime is allocated at batch level and repeated across the five cases; this should not be interpreted as proof of perfectly constant execution time.

12. What does the evidence support?

Supported conclusions

  • LaMa is the strongest descriptive robustness performer across the approved quality anchors and family-balanced ranks.
  • Telea is generally more robust than Stable Diffusion and leads on a minority of variants and anchors.
  • Stable Diffusion is the least robust model descriptively and was never top-ranked across the 75 evaluated mask variants.
  • Preferred-model and anchor-level conclusions can change when only mask placement or geometry changes.
  • No paired model contrast or exploratory morphology association survived FDR correction.
  • Runtime is operational evidence and does not indicate restoration quality.

Limitations

  • Only five paintings are independent experimental units.
  • One painting represents each category, so painting and category effects cannot be separated.
  • Mask family and damaged area are paired and cannot be interpreted independently.
  • The masks are controlled synthetic realizations rather than naturally occurring conservation damage.
  • Stable Diffusion uses one preselected seed per mask; this is not a stochastic uncertainty experiment.

The practical conclusion is binary but scoped: repeating evaluation across mask realizations is necessary when a result may influence model selection. The current experiment supports LaMa as the more dependable computational choice, but it does not prove historical authenticity and is not a conservation approval.

13. Final contribution to the thesis

This experiment extends the thesis from comparing restoration outputs to evaluating whether those comparisons remain stable when a plausible input mask changes.

  • RQ1 — Restoration quality: LaMa was the strongest descriptive performer, Telea was second, and Stable Diffusion was least stable across the approved evidence.
  • RQ2 — Trustworthy evaluation: repeated mask realizations reveal conclusion sensitivity that a single test mask would hide.
  • RQ3 — Explainability and uncertainty: the notebook identifies where conclusions change and which evidence anchors disagree. Input-mask robustness is not calibrated confidence.

Notebook 24 contributes a practical evaluation rule: restoration models should be compared across multiple valid mask realizations whenever mask placement is uncertain. Robustness evidence complements quality, uncertainty, heatmap, and human-review evidence; it does not replace them.
